title: Model-Based Online Decision Making via Generative Trajectory Planning
claim: Our method sits between two paradigms, keeping learned-model reasoning of optimization while using a generative prior to avoid solving optimization from scratch.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, ours in the middle flanked by two baselines
description: Three rounded, dark-blue-bordered panels sit side by side, each with a bold blue serif title. Left, Reinforcement Learning: State s_t flows into a Policy box π(a|s) that outputs Action a_t, with a double-headed arrow linking it to a Critic Q(s,a) box that takes Reward r_t. Middle, Generative Trajectory Planning (ours): State s_t feeds a Diffusion Prior box that outputs an Action Trajectory a_t. A double-headed arrow labeled Planning connects it to a dotted-outline group holding Value Model, Ensemble Dynamics Model and Reward Model boxes. Right, Trajectory Optimization: State s_t feeds an Optimizer box that outputs an Action Trajectory a_t. Diagonal arrows from Dynamics Model and Reward Model point up into the Optimizer. Boxes are pale blue with blue outlines on a white background. The eye goes first to the middle panel, which is the largest.
caption: Generative Trajectory Planning. GTP combines the data-driven nature of RL with the long-horizon reasoning of trajectory optimization. A learned diffusion prior proposes candidate action sequences, which are evaluated and iteratively refined through learned models. By using a generative prior, GTP avoids computational cost of optimization while preserving long-horizon reasoning.
abstract: Online decision-making faces a tension between efficient inference and long-horizon reasoning. Value-based methods rely on short-horizon bootstrapping that limits the propagation of long-term information, while trajectory optimization methods plan explicitly but must solve a high-dimensional optimization problem at every decision step. We propose Generative Trajectory Planning (GTP), a model-based framework that addresses this tension by learning a generative model as a proposal distribution over action sequences. Instead of optimizing sequences from scratch, GTP samples candidate sequences from a diffusion prior and refines them using learned dynamics, reward, and value models, enabling efficient trajectory-level reasoning. Across continuous control and long-horizon manipulation tasks, GTP matches or exceeds state-of-the-art model-free, diffusion-policy, and model-based baselines, and remains stable in regimes where strong baselines degrade. Our results suggest that generative models are best understood not as policies, but as structured proposal distributions for planning, offering a new perspective on how to integrate generative modeling with model-based decision-making.
